answers.children: Yes — Great Danes are good with children thanks to their patient and gentle nature that allows them to tolerate toddlers climbing over them without reaction. Their imposing build means they lean heavily for affection and can knock over small children by accident, while their history as estate guardians makes them calm around family. The breed forms tight bonds and wants to stay near its people constantly. (PawLabs child-friendly score: 7/10)
answers.other-pets: Yes — Great Danes generally get along with other pets because their friendly temperament leads them to lick rather than show aggression. Their massive size can overwhelm smaller animals during play and their protective instincts from boar-hunting ancestry may create wariness toward unfamiliar dogs, though they remain sociable with household companions.
answers.exercise: Great Danes need two moderate 30-minute walks daily plus some low-impact backyard play. Their giant frame and history as nimble boar hunters mean excess strain on growing joints can cause lifelong problems, while insufficient activity leads to restlessness that turns into indoor destruction such as chewing furniture. Adults mellow and require little beyond steady gentle movement.
answers.shedding: Yes — Great Danes shed moderately with short smooth coats that release hair year-round onto furniture and clothing. The single-layer coat lacks feathering or undercoat density so it does not mat yet still produces visible dustings that demand regular sweeping, especially from a dog that leans against walls and furniture at 28-32 inches tall.
answers.hypoallergenic: No breed is hypoallergenic and Great Danes are not among those commonly suggested for allergy sufferers. Their short smooth coat still releases dander and moderate levels of hair that can trigger reactions despite the lack of heavy double coat or seasonal blow.
answers.training: Great Danes are moderately easy to train because their patient and intelligent nature responds to consistent direction without high independence. Bred originally as guards and companions rather than independent hunters they remain biddable yet their giant size makes them hard to correct physically once they lean or follow owners from room to room.
answers.lifespan: Great Danes live 7-10 years. Their giant build and short clock bring significant health concerns that accompany the massive frame refined in Germany for both power and elegance, while high food and care costs reflect the demands of maintaining such a towering companion throughout its relatively brief life.
answers.size: Great Danes reach 110-175 lb and stand 28-32 in at the shoulder. Their substantial mastiff-derived build means they rest chins on kitchen counters without stretching and lean with enough weight to knock adults off balance, turning everyday life into a constant navigation of oversized affectionate presence that fills rooms and furniture.
answers.barking: Great Danes do not bark a lot. Their imposing presence as a deterrent to intruders means they stay quiet most of the time yet may bark once at delivery people before immediately wagging their tail, reflecting a calm temperament refined from medieval boar-hound courage into modern gentle guardianship.
answers.apartment: Yes — Great Danes can live in an apartment because their low energy and patient demeanor let them settle calmly indoors after moderate walks. Their size makes them surprisingly low-noise companions that rarely bark yet the sheer bulk requires careful movement around furniture and the high food costs remain unchanged by living space.
answers.first-time: No — Great Danes are not a good first dog because their giant size brings high food and care costs along with the need to manage accidental leaning and short lifespan realities that challenge novices. Their affectionate following behaviour and vulnerable joints during puppy bursts demand experience to avoid unintentional household chaos or over-exercise.
